questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.1 (Kinematics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, projectile motion, relative velocity)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: Three of the five keys depend on separating what is shared from what is not: the horizontal component survives at the top of a flight, complementary launch angles share a range but not a flight time, and a velocity-proportional drag leaves the vertical motion of a horizontally fired ball untouched. Each distractor collapses one of those separations.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on kinematics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A projectile is launched from level ground at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $40^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path?

options.label: A
options.rationale: At the highest point the vertical component of the velocity is zero, so the speed is just the unchanged horizontal component $30\cos 40^{\circ}$, which is $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This keeps the launch speed, forgetting that the horizontal component is only part of it and that the vertical part has been removed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the vertical component $30\sin 40^{\circ}$, which is the part reduced to zero at the top rather than the part that survives.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This treats the highest point as an instant of rest, confusing the vertical component with the whole velocity vector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two projectiles are launched from the same point at the same speed, one at an angle $\theta$ and the other at $90^{\circ}-\theta$, where $\theta \ne 45^{\circ}$. Both land at the launch height. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both have the same range, but the projectile launched at the larger angle is in the air for longer.
options.rationale: The range depends on $\sin 2\theta$, which takes the same value for complementary angles, while the flight time depends on $\sin\theta$, so the steeper launch stays up longer.

options.label: B
options.text: Both are in the air for the same time, but the projectile launched at the larger angle travels further.
options.rationale: This reverses the two results: the flight times differ because the vertical components differ, and the ranges do not.

options.label: C
options.text: The steeper launch has both the greater range and the greater time of flight.
options.rationale: The time claim is right but the range claim is wrong, because complementary angles share the same value of $\sin 2\theta$.

options.label: D
options.text: The shallower launch has the greater range and the greater time of flight.
options.rationale: Both claims are inverted: the shallower launch is in the air for the shorter time, and neither launch has the greater range.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A ball is released from rest at the same instant that an identical ball at the same height is fired horizontally. Both balls experience air resistance with a drag force proportional to their speed. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both balls reach the ground at the same time.
options.rationale: When the drag force is proportional to velocity the component equations separate, so the vertical motion is unaffected by how fast the ball is moving horizontally and both balls fall identically.

options.label: B
options.text: The fired ball lands later, because the drag opposing its horizontal motion also slows its descent.
options.rationale: Drag opposes the velocity vector, and for drag proportional to speed each component of the drag depends only on that component of the velocity.

options.label: C
options.text: The dropped ball lands later, because it has the lower speed and so experiences less drag.
options.rationale: The drag acts on each velocity component separately, so the total speed of the ball is irrelevant to how fast it falls.

options.label: D
options.text: The fired ball lands later, because it travels along a longer path.
options.rationale: Path length does not determine the fall time; only the vertical motion does, and the two vertical motions are identical.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A particle moves along a straight line at $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and then at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction for $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What are its average speed and its average velocity over the $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The distance travelled is $32\ \mathrm{m}$ and the displacement is $16\ \mathrm{m}$, so dividing each by $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$ gives $6.4$ and $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ respectively.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This swaps the two definitions, dividing displacement by time to obtain a speed and distance by time to obtain a velocity.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This divides distance by time twice, ignoring that the second stage partly undoes the displacement gained in the first.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The velocity is right but the speed takes the unweighted mean of the two speeds instead of weighting each by the time it applies.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A boat whose speed in still water is $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ must cross a river $120\ \mathrm{m}$ wide in which the current flows at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the shortest possible crossing time, and how far downstream does the boat land?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Pointing the boat straight across maximises the cross-river component at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, giving $30\ \mathrm{s}$, during which the current carries the boat $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstream.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The drift is right but the time belongs to a different aim; the crossing time is set only by the cross-river component of the boat's velocity.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This assumes the current can be cancelled at no cost, but cancelling it uses part of the boat's speed and therefore lengthens the crossing.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the time for the shortest path rather than the shortest time, so it correctly describes a different journey and answers a different question.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** Resolve the launch velocity: the horizontal component is $30\cos 40^{\circ}=22.98$ and the vertical component is $30\sin 40^{\circ}=19.28$. The horizontal component is constant throughout, and at the highest point the vertical component has been reduced to zero by gravity, so the speed there is simply $22.98$, i.e. $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(A1)** The near miss is C, which reports the component that has vanished rather than the one that remains.

**(b) A.** The range is $v^{2}\sin 2\theta/g$, and $\sin\bigl(2(90^{\circ}-\theta)\bigr)=\sin(180^{\circ}-2\theta)=\sin 2\theta$, so the two ranges are equal. The flight time is $2v\sin\theta/g$, which is larger for the larger angle. **(A1)** Distractor D inverts both conclusions and C gets only the time right.

**(c) A.** With drag $\mathbf{F}=-k\mathbf{v}$ the component equations are separate: vertically, $m\dot v_{y}=-kv_{y}-mg$ for both balls, with the same initial condition $v_{y}=0$. The horizontal motion therefore cannot influence the descent, and both land together. **(A1)** This is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and B, C and D are all attempts to make the longer or faster trajectory cost time.

**(d) A.** Distance $=8.0(3.0)+4.0(2.0)=24+8=32\ \mathrm{m}$; displacement $=24-8=16\ \mathrm{m}$. Dividing by $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$ gives an average speed of $6.4$ and an average velocity of $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(A1)** The pair is what is being tested: many candidates compute one correctly and then quote it twice.

**(e) A.** The crossing time is the width divided by the component of the boat's velocity perpendicular to the bank. That component is greatest, at the full $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, when the boat points straight across, so $t=120/4.0=30\ \mathrm{s}$ and the drift is $3.0\times30=90\ \mathrm{m}$. **(A1)** D is the trap: $45\ \mathrm{s}$ and landing opposite is a correct calculation of the *shortest path*, since the resultant speed is then $\sqrt{4.0^{2}-3.0^{2}}=2.65\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $120/2.65=45\ \mathrm{s}$, but the question asks for the shortest time.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $23.0$ or $23.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (b) The reasoning mark is implicit in the key: a candidate who states equal ranges but equal times has not earned it. (c) This is the hardest item in the cluster and the one most likely to be guessed wrong; accept any answer that identifies the independence of the components, and note that the result would be different for drag proportional to the square of the speed, where the components no longer separate and the fired ball would in fact land later. (d) Accept fractions; the unit mark is not separate here. (e) Award no follow-through from a mistaken minimum-time aim: the $45\ \mathrm{s}$ figure belongs to a different optimisation and using it for the drift gives $135\ \mathrm{m}$, which is not offered. Candidates who eliminate C and D first, on the grounds that cancelling the current must cost time, are using the strongest route to the key.
questions.explanation:
This cluster is built around one idea: in kinematics, the first move is always to decide which quantities are shared and which are not. In (a) the horizontal component survives and the vertical one does not. In (b) complementary launch angles share a range because the range depends on $\sin 2\theta$, but they do not share a flight time because that depends on $\sin\theta$. In (c) a horizontally fired ball shares its entire vertical motion with a dropped one, and the surprise is that this remains true when linear drag is present, because the drag then acts independently on each component. That last point is the conceptual peak of the cluster: most students have been taught the vacuum case and assume that adding air resistance must break the tie, when in fact it depends on the drag law.

Items (d) and (e) target the same separation instinct in a computational setting. In (d) the distance and the displacement differ by $16\ \mathrm{m}$, and a candidate who computes only one of them halves the question. In (e) the shortest time and the shortest path are different journeys, and the boat cannot achieve both; the $45\ \mathrm{s}$ option is a correct calculation of the wrong thing, which is the most reliable way to separate a candidate who has understood the vector structure from one who has only memorised a formula. A guessing student has no easy route here, because the four options in (e) are all internally consistent descriptions of a real journey.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. The distractor set was built from the error patterns recorded for this subtopic: reporting the component that vanishes, swapping distance with displacement, and computing the shortest path when the shortest time is asked for.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: resolve the velocity into components and decide which is constant
identify the quantity that is shared between the two cases being compared
apply the independence of perpendicular motions to the falling and firing cases
separate distance from displacement before dividing by the total time
optimise the required quantity rather than a related one

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.2 (Forces and momentum: Newton's laws, momentum and impulse, conservation of momentum)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: Each key requires a quantity to be reconstructed before it can be used: the normal reaction is reduced by the upward pull of the applied force, the impulse is the area of a triangular force-time graph, the cable tension must accelerate the passenger as well as the lift, and the terminal speed scales with the square of the radius because Stokes drag is linear in radius while weight is cubic.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on forces and momentum. Each one stands alone. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and give each answer to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block of mass $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal surface and is pulled by a force of $15\ \mathrm{N}$ acting at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. The coefficient of dynamic friction is $0.25$. What is the acceleration of the block?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The pull has an upward vertical component of $7.5\ \mathrm{N}$, so the normal reaction is $19.62-7.5=12.12\ \mathrm{N}$, the friction is $3.03\ \mathrm{N}$, and the net horizontal force of $9.96\ \mathrm{N}$ gives $4.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This takes the normal reaction to equal the weight, ignoring that the angled pull lifts the block and so reduces the friction.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This divides the horizontal component of the pull by the mass and omits the friction opposing the motion altogether.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This adds the vertical component of the pull to the weight instead of subtracting it, so the friction is overestimated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two trolleys of mass $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ are held together on a frictionless track by a compressed spring. The spring is released and the $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley moves off at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the speed of the other trolley?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The total momentum was zero and stays zero, so the two momenta are equal in magnitude: $1.5\times3.0=2.5\,v$, giving $1.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This inverts the mass ratio, multiplying by $2.5/1.5$ instead of dividing by it.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This assumes the two trolleys move apart at equal speeds, which would only conserve momentum if their masses were equal.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This conserves kinetic energy instead of momentum, which is wrong because the spring released stored energy during the separation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A force acting on a ball of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ rises uniformly from zero to $60\ \mathrm{N}$ in $0.020\ \mathrm{s}$ and then falls uniformly back to zero over the next $0.040\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the change in speed of the ball?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The impulse is the area under the triangular force-time graph, $\tfrac12(0.060)(60)=1.8\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, and dividing by the mass gives a change in speed of $3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses the area of the enclosing rectangle rather than the triangle, so the impulse is doubled.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This reports the impulse itself as if it were a change in speed, omitting the division by the mass.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This takes the area of only the rising part of the graph, ignoring the longer falling section.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A lift of mass $400\ \mathrm{kg}$ carries a passenger of mass $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ and accelerates upwards at $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. What is the tension in the supporting cable?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The cable must support the total weight of $460\ \mathrm{kg}$ and provide the upward acceleration, so $T=460(9.81+1.2)=5065\ \mathrm{N}$, which is $5.06\ \mathrm{kN}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the total weight alone and ignores the acceleration entirely, as though the lift were moving at constant speed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This subtracts the acceleration from $g$ instead of adding it, which would be right for a lift accelerating downwards.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This applies the acceleration to the lift but not to the passenger, treating only part of the load as being accelerated.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A small sphere falling through a viscous liquid reaches a terminal speed $v$. A second sphere of the same material and twice the radius is dropped into the same liquid. The drag force is given by Stokes' law, $F=6\pi\eta r v$. What is the terminal speed of the larger sphere?

options.label: A
options.rationale: At terminal speed the net weight balances the drag; the net weight scales as the cube of the radius while Stokes drag scales as the radius, so the terminal speed scales as radius squared and doubles in radius gives four times the speed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This makes the terminal speed proportional to the radius, which would follow if the driving force were also proportional to the radius.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This scales with the cube of the radius, keeping the weight but ignoring that the drag force itself grows with radius.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This treats terminal speed as a property of the material, independent of size, which is only true if both the driving and the resisting force scale the same way.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** Resolve the pull: the horizontal component is $15\cos30^{\circ}=12.99\ \mathrm{N}$ and the vertical component is $15\sin30^{\circ}=7.50\ \mathrm{N}$ upwards. The normal reaction is therefore $mg-7.50=19.62-7.50=12.12\ \mathrm{N}$, not $mg$. Friction is $0.25\times12.12=3.03\ \mathrm{N}$, so the net horizontal force is $12.99-3.03=9.96\ \mathrm{N}$ and $a=9.96/2.0=4.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. **(A1)** The whole question turns on the normal reaction; B is what you get by taking it as $mg$.

**(b) A.** The initial momentum is zero and no external horizontal force acts, so $1.5(3.0)+2.5(-v)=0$ and $v=1.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction. **(A1)** D is the interesting wrong answer: conserving kinetic energy gives $\tfrac12(1.5)(9)=\tfrac12(2.5)v^{2}$, so $v=2.32$, but the spring releases stored energy, so kinetic energy is *not* conserved here.

**(c) A.** The impulse is the area under the force-time graph. The shape is a triangle of base $0.020+0.040=0.060\ \mathrm{s}$ and height $60\ \mathrm{N}$, so the impulse is $\tfrac12(0.060)(60)=1.8\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and $\Delta v=1.8/0.50=3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(A1)** B doubles it by using the rectangle, and C forgets to divide by the mass.

**(d) A.** Treating the lift and passenger as one body of mass $460\ \mathrm{kg}$: $T-460g=460(1.2)$, so $T=460(11.01)=5065\ \mathrm{N}=5.06\ \mathrm{kN}$. **(A1)** The mark is for including the passenger in the accelerated mass; D, at $4.99\ \mathrm{kN}$, is the result of accelerating only the lift.

**(e) A.** At terminal speed, net weight equals drag: $(\rho_{s}-\rho_{l})\tfrac43\pi r^{3}g=6\pi\eta r v$, so $v\propto r^{2}$. Doubling $r$ multiplies $v$ by $4$. **(A1)** The two scalings are the point: the driving force is cubic in $r$ and the resisting force is linear in $r$, so the ratio grows as $r^{2}$.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $4.9$ to $5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; a candidate who writes the normal reaction as $12.1\ \mathrm{N}$ has the key idea even if the final figure slips. (b) The direction is not asked for and should not be penalised, but a candidate who says the trolleys move in the same direction has not conserved momentum. (c) Accept $3.6$ or $3.60$; watch for the candidate who computes the area correctly but then multiplies by the mass instead of dividing. (d) Accept $5.05$ to $5.07\ \mathrm{kN}$; the distinction between B, C and D is entirely about which mass is accelerated and in which direction, so an unannotated correct figure earns the mark but a wrong figure earns nothing. (e) This is a scaling question and no numerical value is needed; accept any answer that correctly states that the terminal speed is proportional to the square of the radius. Note that the answer would be different for drag proportional to $v^{2}$, which is the more common regime for large spheres in air.
questions.explanation:
Every item in this cluster hides a quantity that has to be reconstructed before the familiar formula can be applied. In (a) it is the normal reaction, which the angled pull reduces below the weight; in (c) it is the impulse, which is an area and not a force; in (d) it is the accelerated mass, which includes the passenger; in (e) it is the scaling of the driving force against the scaling of the resisting force. A candidate who reaches straight for $F=ma$ or $p=mv$ without building the missing quantity lands on a distractor, and the distractors are placed exactly where those shortcuts lead.

Two of the five contain a second, deeper trap. In (b) the natural instinct is to conserve kinetic energy, because that is what is usually conserved in the problems students meet; here the spring is an internal energy source, so only momentum is conserved, and the $2.32\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ option is there for exactly that error. In (e) the instinct is to say the bigger sphere falls faster by a factor of two or eight, and only a candidate who writes both scalings down finds the factor of four. The cluster therefore discriminates on whether a student checks the applicability of a conservation law and the dimensions of a scaling, rather than on whether they can substitute into a formula.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Distractors were built from the four error patterns that dominate this subtopic: taking the normal reaction as the weight, conserving the wrong quantity, confusing an impulse with a force, and applying a cubic scaling to a linear drag law.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: resolve the applied force and rebuild the normal reaction before using friction
decide which conservation law applies and apply it to the whole system
take the impulse as the area under the force-time graph and divide by mass
apply Newton's second law to the combined accelerated mass
compare how the driving force and the drag force each scale with radius

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Substitute the given numbers straight into the standard formula for each quantity and read the answer off the calculator.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Several of the keys need a quantity that is not given and has to be built first, such as a normal reaction reduced by the vertical component of the applied force, or an impulse obtained as the area under a triangular force-time graph.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Answers obtained from the given numbers alone, with the normal reaction taken as the full weight and the impulse taken as the product of the peak force and the total time.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.4 (Thermodynamics: first law, internal energy, work, heat engine efficiency, second law)
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The first law is a signed statement about three quantities and every distractor is a sign or a missing term: an adiabatic change is not one in which nothing happens, the actual efficiency and the Carnot efficiency answer different questions, and isothermal expansion does a logarithmic rather than a linear amount of work.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on thermodynamics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Throughout, take the gas to be ideal unless a question says otherwise, and remember that the first law relates the change in internal energy to both the thermal energy transferred and the work done. Use $R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ where it is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas is compressed adiabatically. Which statement about the gas is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Its internal energy increases by an amount equal to the work done on it.
options.rationale: Adiabatic means no heat enters or leaves, so the first law reduces to the change in internal energy being equal to the work done on the gas, and the temperature rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Its internal energy is unchanged, because no heat is transferred.
options.rationale: This confuses adiabatic with isothermal; work is still done on the gas, and that work raises the internal energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Work is done by the gas and its internal energy falls.
options.rationale: This describes an adiabatic expansion, not a compression, so both the sign of the work and the change in internal energy are reversed.

options.label: D
options.text: Its temperature is unchanged, because the process is adiabatic.
options.rationale: A constant temperature in a gas usually requires heat to flow, which is precisely what an adiabatic change forbids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A gas absorbs $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of thermal energy and expands, doing $200\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

options.label: A
options.rationale: With the sign convention that work done by the gas is positive, the first law gives a change in internal energy of $500-200=300\ \mathrm{J}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This adds the work instead of subtracting it, treating work done by the gas as though it were further energy supplied to the gas.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong; the gas absorbs more energy as heat than it loses by doing work.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This ignores the work term altogether and equates the change in internal energy with the heat supplied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A heat engine takes in $900\ \mathrm{J}$ from a reservoir at $600\ \mathrm{K}$ and rejects heat to a reservoir at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. It does $300\ \mathrm{J}$ of work in each cycle. What are its actual efficiency and the maximum efficiency possible between these temperatures?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The actual efficiency is the work output divided by the heat input, $300/900=33\%$, while the Carnot limit is one minus the ratio of the reservoir temperatures, $1-300/600=50\%$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The actual efficiency is right but the limit uses the ratio of temperatures the wrong way round, giving the complement of the Carnot value.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This swaps the two quantities, reporting the Carnot limit as the achieved efficiency.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This subtracts the achieved efficiency from one, reporting the fraction of the input energy that is rejected rather than the fraction that is converted to work.

parts.label: d
parts.text: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ from a volume $V$ to a volume $2V$. How much work is done by the gas?

options.label: A
options.rationale: For an isothermal change the work is $nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 8.31\times300\times\ln 2 = 1728\ \mathrm{J}$, which is $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is $nRT$ alone and omits the logarithm that comes from integrating the falling pressure over the expansion.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This takes half of $nRT$, treating the pressure as though it fell linearly with volume so that an average pressure could be used.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This confuses an isothermal change with an isochoric one; a constant temperature does not mean a constant volume.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which of the following processes is permitted by the second law of thermodynamics?

options.label: A
options.text: A gas expanding into an evacuated chamber with no other change anywhere.
options.rationale: Free expansion is irreversible and therefore allowed; the entropy of the gas increases, so the second law is satisfied rather than violated.

options.label: B
options.text: Thermal energy flowing spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body with no other change.
options.rationale: This is the Clausius statement of the second law and is forbidden; such a transfer is only possible if work is supplied, as in a refrigerator.

options.label: C
options.text: A heat engine converting all the thermal energy it absorbs into work over a complete cycle.
options.rationale: This is the Kelvin statement of the second law and is forbidden; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir.

options.label: D
options.text: The total entropy of an isolated system decreasing.
options.rationale: The entropy of an isolated system can never decrease; it stays constant for a reversible change and increases for an irreversible one.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** Adiabatic means $Q=0$, so the first law $\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}}$ becomes $\Delta U = -W_{\text{by}} = W_{\text{on}}$. Compressing the gas means work is done *on* it, so $\Delta U>0$ and the temperature rises. **(A1)** B confuses adiabatic with isothermal and D then inherits that confusion.

**(b) A.** With $W_{\text{by}}=+200\ \mathrm{J}$ and $Q=+500\ \mathrm{J}$, $\Delta U = 500-200=+300\ \mathrm{J}$. **(A1)** The sign convention is the whole question: B adds, C keeps the magnitude but flips the sign.

**(c) A.** The achieved efficiency is $\eta = W/Q_{\text{in}} = 300/900 = 0.333$. The Carnot limit depends only on the reservoir temperatures: $\eta_{C}=1-T_{C}/T_{H}=1-300/600=0.500$. **(A1)** The two numbers answer different questions and D, at $67\%$, comes from subtracting the achieved efficiency from one and so reporting the rejected fraction of the input as if it were the useful output.

**(d) A.** For an isothermal change $pV=nRT$ is constant, so $W=\int p\,dV = nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 8.31\times300\times\ln 2 = 1.73\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$. **(A1)** B is $nRT$ with the logarithm omitted, and C treats the pressure as falling linearly so that a mean pressure could be used.

**(e) A.** Free expansion into a vacuum does no work and involves no heat transfer, so $\Delta U=0$ for an ideal gas, but the entropy increases because the gas occupies a larger volume. The second law forbids the other three: B is the Clausius statement, C is the Kelvin statement, and D contradicts the entropy form directly. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any answer that identifies the internal energy as increasing by the work done on the gas. (b) Candidates using the opposite sign convention consistently, so that work done on the gas is positive, should still be credited if their arithmetic and conclusion match their convention. (c) Accept $33$ or $33.3\%$ and $50\%$; a candidate who quotes the Carnot value as the achieved efficiency has not distinguished the two ideas and earns nothing. (d) Accept $1.7$ to $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$; note that $\ln 2$ is the only place a logarithm appears in this subtopic and it is frequently forgotten. (e) Accept any correct statement of why free expansion is permitted; a candidate who says it is permitted because no heat flows has the right answer for the wrong reason, since the decisive point is that the entropy increases. Note that B and C are both statements of the second law rather than the first, so a candidate who justifies rejecting them by saying energy would not be conserved has used the wrong law and should not be credited. Candidates often find (e) the hardest item despite it requiring no calculation, because it asks which process is permitted rather than which is forbidden; three of the four options are familiar prohibitions, so the correct answer looks wrong at first reading.
questions.explanation:
This cluster exists because the first law of thermodynamics is a signed equation in three quantities and students routinely lose marks on the signs rather than on the physics. Items (a) and (b) isolate exactly that: in (a) the compression means the work term enters with the opposite sign to an expansion, and in (b) the gas both receives heat and spends energy doing work, so the change in internal energy is the difference, not the sum. The distractors are the four ways of getting a sign wrong.

Items (c) and (d) isolate a different and more interesting confusion: the difference between what a device actually achieves and what is theoretically available. In (c) the engine's real efficiency and the Carnot efficiency are computed from entirely different information, one from the energy flows and the other from the reservoir temperatures alone, and a candidate who reaches for the temperatures to compute the achieved efficiency has conflated them. In (d) the work of an isothermal expansion is logarithmic, which surprises students who expect a pressure-times-volume product; the $2.49\ \mathrm{kJ}$ distractor is $nRT$ and the $1.25\ \mathrm{kJ}$ distractor is the mean-pressure approximation that would be correct if the pressure fell linearly with volume, which it does not. Item (e) closes the cluster by asking which process the second law permits, and the correct answer is the one that increases entropy, which is the unifying idea behind the whole cluster.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Distractors were constructed from the sign and missing-term errors characteristic of this subtopic: adiabatic treated as isothermal, work added rather than subtracted, actual efficiency confused with the Carnot bound, and the logarithm of an isothermal expansion omitted.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: identify which of heat and work is zero from the name of the process
apply the first law with the sign convention fixed by whether the gas expands
distinguish the achieved efficiency from the Carnot bound on the reservoir temperatures
integrate the equation of state for an isothermal change rather than using a mean pressure
test each proposed process against the entropy statement of the second law
